t: Minimum Operations to Make Columns Strictly Increasing — Greedy Sweep
o: Only increments are allowed, and columns must become strictly increasing top to bottom, independently per column. Greedy per column: keep the smallest achievable value consistent with the previous row. For grid [[3,2],[1,3],[3,4],[0,1]] column 0 needs 3+2+6 = 11 operations and column 1 needs 4, totaling 15. Because increments only push values up, raising a cell to exactly prev+1 is always optimal — anything higher wastes operations and constrains later rows more.
k: Columns are independent; within a column, set each cell to max(cell, prev+1) and charge the increase — greedy optimality follows from monotonicity.

a.i: Transpose mentally and sweep each column top-down maintaining prev (the enforced value of the previous row). If the current cell is <= prev, pay prev+1-cell operations and set prev = prev+1; otherwise prev = cell. The sum of payments is minimal since any valid assignment has each value at least this greedy choice (induction down the column).
s: Walk rows: if v <= prev, add prev+1-v to the answer and set prev = prev+1; else set prev = v.
a.t: O(m*n) — each cell is visited exactly once per column sweep.
a.sp: O(1) — a single running prev per column.

w: Greedy exchange argument: lifting a cell any higher than prev+1 only increases the cost now and raises the floor for all later cells, so matching prev+1 exactly dominates. Pitfalls: using prev = v when v > prev but forgetting the strictly-increasing requirement at equality (v == prev must also be bumped), and overflowing the operation count in languages with fixed ints (max ~50*2500 fits in int, but use long to be safe). Edge cases: single-row matrices (zero operations), constant columns. Follow-up: allow decrements too (then it becomes an L1-isotonic-regression style problem), or require strictly increasing rows as well.
